content: Studies comparing the effects of dance interventions to other forms of physical training or no intervention in patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD) were analyzed. The outcomes assessed included motor symptoms using the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale III (UPDRS III), functional mobility using the Timed Up and Go Test (TUG), endurance using the 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT), freezing of gait using the Freezing of Gait Questionnaire (FOG-Q), walking velocity using GAITRite, and quality of life using the Parkinson’s Disease Questionnaire (PDQ-39). Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the methodological quality of the studies. Results were presented as weighted mean differences. Results: Five randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 159 patients were included. Dance interventions significantly improved UPDRS III scores and reduced TUG times compared to other exercise types. When compared to no intervention, dance also led to significant improvements in motor scores. Conclusion: Dance interventions can enhance motor parameters and functional mobility in patients with Parkinson’s disease. RCTs included patients at any stage of PD, of any age and gender, who participated in dance interventions lasting at least three weeks. These studies analyzed functional and biomechanical gait parameters and quality of life outcomes. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Kalyani et al. (2019) evaluated the effects of dance on gait, cognition, and dual-tasking in Parkinson’s disease. Eligible studies included individuals with PD who underwent dance-based interventions and reported outcomes related to gait, cognition, or dual-tasking. Of 1,079 articles initially identified, 25 were retained, and 12 had sufficient data for meta-analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane tool. Dance interventions significantly improved gait speed, TUG performance, freezing of gait, and 6MWT times compared to controls. However, evidence on the optimal intensity, frequency, duration, or music type for dance interventions was limited. Findings should be interpreted cautiously due to the lack of RCTs and moderate-to-high risk of bias in the studies. Overall, dance may improve PD symptoms, particularly gait, global cognition, and dual-tasking. Another systematic review by Stuckenschneider et al. (2019) compared the effects of different exercise modes on cognitive function in Parkinson’s disease. Eleven RCTs involving 508 patients (mean age 68 years) were included. Aerobic exercise showed a tendency to improve memory, but no clear effect of exercise mode was identified. All exercise modes were associated with improved cognitive function, with executive function showing the most significant improvement. The study emphasized the need for future trials to determine the most effective exercise protocols. A meta-analysis by Bonini-Rocha et al. (2018) examined the effectiveness of circuit-based exercises on gait speed, balance, and functional mobility in stroke patients. Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria, and eight provided data for meta-analysis. Circuit-based exercises were more effective than conventional interventions for improving gait speed but showed no significant advantage in balance or functional mobility. The authors concluded that circuit-based exercises are beneficial for gait improvement but not superior to conventional methods for other outcomes. Boyne et al. (2017) conducted a meta-analysis to assess the impact of aerobic exercise (AEX) on fitness and walking capacity post-stroke. AEX significantly improved aerobic capacity, walking speed, and endurance. Higher AEX intensity and baseline fitness levels were associated with better outcomes. Walking-based AEX was more effective than seated AEX for walking outcomes. The study highlighted the need for task-specific AEX to improve walking speed and endurance. Cugusi et al. (2017) reviewed the effects of Nordic walking (NW) on cardiovascular disease rehabilitation. Fifteen RCTs were included, with eight entering the meta-analysis. NW combined with conventional cardiovascular rehabilitation (CCVR) improved functional capacity and quality of life compared to CCVR alone. However, no significant differences were observed in heart failure patients. The authors suggested that NW is a promising activity for cardiovascular rehabilitation but requires further research. Ge et al. (2017) conducted a meta-analysis on the effects of traditional Chinese exercises (TCEs) on limb function in stroke patients. Thirty-one RCTs with 2,349 participants were included. TCEs improved limb motor function, balance, activities of daily living (ADL), and neurological impairment. However, no benefits were observed for physical function on the Short Physical Performance Battery or 2-Minute Step Test. The authors recommended further high-quality RCTs to confirm these findings. Hendrey et al. (2018) reviewed resistance training protocols for mobility improvement post-stroke and their adherence to American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) guidelines. Thirty-nine trials were included, with adherence to frequency being high (100%) but low for intensity (32%) and specificity (24%). Finally, Ilunga Tshiswaka et al. (2018) reviewed walking training interventions for stroke survivors. Interventions involving treadmill walking with auditory stimulation showed significant improvements compared to overground walking. The study highlighted the importance of improving physical function to enhance independence among stroke survivors and called for more research on the interaction between physical function and socialization. Li et al. (2018) investigated the effects of Tai Chi on balance and gait in stroke survivors. Five RCTs with 346 patients were included. Tai Chi showed short-term benefits for gait ability, but further large-scale, long-term RCTs are needed to confirm these findings. Miranda and Marques (2018) reviewed the effects of Pilates on non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including cardiovascular diseases, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases, and diabetes. The review found strong evidence for Pilates improving exercise tolerance and physical function in individuals with chronic conditions. However, further research is needed to systematize evidence across NCDs.
